title: Business intelligence and semantic delivery
summary: Plan Cinderline's morning quality page from the decision it serves: defensible labels, tiles bound to one metric contract, filters and parameters, two access doors, freshness in words, a metric view, the business-user surface, external BI tools, a storyboard and an acceptance script.
objectives: Write a page's decision chain and label a rate tile with axis, units, period, denominator and freshness, bound to a named metric contract.
Predict the effect of field filters and parameters, and write an access matrix separating dashboard permissions, the publish-time data-permission choice and table privileges.

State freshness in words, order the refresh after the job, and place metric views, Genie One and Power BI, Tableau and ODBC or JDBC clients against the same page, ending with a storyboard and an acceptance script.

Try it: the supplier asks for line 2

questions.prompt: Line 4 had no accepted inspections on day 5. Which rendering of its tile satisfies the unit_defect_rate contract?

options.text: The words "no inspections", produced from a NULL rate.
options.rationale: The contract says a line with no accepted inspections has no rate; the dataset returns NULL and the tile renders it in words.

options.text: 0.0%, because no defective units were found.
options.rationale: 0.0% asserts a perfect day that never happened, and would rank line 4 best in a meeting that chooses where to look.

options.text: No tile at all for line 4 that day.
options.rationale: A vanished tile hides the fact that the line did not run; the published table keeps a row for every line in the line list, so the line is shown.

options.text: The average of the other three lines' rates.
options.rationale: An imputed value presents a number the contract never defines, and a mean of rates is forbidden even for the plant figure.

questions.prompt: Cinderline's supplier contact asks to see line 2's defect rate in the supplier's Tableau. Which delivery keeps the access matrix and the contract intact?

options.text: Grant the supplier's connection identity SELECT on a view returning only line 2, and add its own acceptance row and a freshness caption in Tableau.
options.rationale: The Tableau connection runs as its own identity, so the catalog grant is the wall; the report needs its own labels and acceptance because nothing of the page travels.

options.text: Share the AI/BI page with Can View and set the line filter's default to 2.
options.rationale: A filter is a reading aid, not a wall; under shared data permissions every row the datasets return is reachable by changing the filter.

options.text: Grant SELECT on accepted.daily_line_rate and ask the supplier to filter to line 2.
options.rationale: That exposes every line's rate to the supplier; the restriction would depend on the supplier's goodwill rather than a grant.

options.text: Email a CSV export of the page every morning.
options.rationale: An export has no contract binding, no freshness line and no access control after it leaves; it is a copy nobody can revoke.

questions.prompt: Two dashboards print different plant defect rates for the same day. Which change stops them computing the plant rate differently?

options.text: Define unit_defect_rate once as a measure in a metric view and base both dashboards' datasets on it.
options.rationale: The ratio of sums then lives in one governed definition, recomputed for each grouping, so neither dashboard can average line rates.

options.text: Round both tiles to one decimal place.
options.rationale: Rounding hides a small disagreement without removing the two different calculations behind it.

options.text: Add a description to each tile saying how it was computed.
options.rationale: Documentation of two formulas leaves two formulas; the readers still see two numbers.

options.text: Set both plant widgets to AVERAGE over the per-line rate column.
options.rationale: That makes them agree on the wrong figure, the mean of rates the contract forbids.

cards.prompt: Before drawing any tile, which four things does a dashboard plan write down first?
cards.answer: The audience, the decision they make from the page, the action that follows, and the metric that changes that decision.
cards.explanation: A page designed from the tables at hand fills up with tiles nobody acts on. Writing the chain first, for example supervisors at 8 a.m., which line to investigate, send a technician, unit_defect_rate per line, lets every proposed tile be tested: a tile on no link of the chain is removed or marked unverified.

cards.prompt: A tile reads "Defects 4.8" over bars whose axis starts at 4.0, with no date on the page. What must its label add?
cards.answer: The unit and denominator, the period covered, the contract name and version, the publish time, and an axis from zero or a stated truncation.
cards.explanation: Each missing part lets a reader draw a different conclusion from the same value: a count or a rate, yesterday or a rolling week, a 4 per cent move drawn as a bar a third taller, and no way to tell whether yesterday is in the numbers. Reading the label aloud as a sentence exposes the gap.

cards.prompt: Four lines inspected 300, 250, 250 and 240 units with 10, 15, 12 and 10 defective. What should the plant tile show, and why not 4.6%?
cards.answer: It should show 47 over 1,040, which is 4.5%; 4.6% is the mean of the four line rates, which the contract forbids.
cards.explanation: The contract defines the plant rate as the same calculation over all lines, summing numerators and denominators before dividing. Averaging rates weights a 240-unit line like a 300-unit line, so a widget set to AVERAGE on a rate column prints a number no contract defines and a careful reader will catch.

cards.prompt: A supervisor changes the business-day parameter rather than the line filter. Why do every line tile and the plant tile move?
cards.answer: Because a parameter is substituted into each dataset's SQL before aggregation, so every connected query recomputes for the new day.
cards.explanation: A field filter only narrows rows a dataset already returned, which is why the plant dataset, having no line field, ignores the line filter. A parameter changes the WHERE clause itself, so the sums and the rates are recomputed over a different population in every dataset that uses it.

cards.prompt: Why does raising a supervisor to Can Manage on the page not fix tiles that fail under individual data permissions?
cards.answer: Can Manage opens more of the dashboard object; the tiles fail because the supervisor lacks the table grants (USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and SELECT), which are separate.
cards.explanation: The dashboard's permission levels govern viewing, running, editing and managing the page. Whether a query returns rows is decided by data permissions on the underlying objects for the identity the query runs as, and under individual data permissions that identity is the viewer, so only the matrix's grants on the objects the page reads help.

cards.prompt: A page is published with shared data permissions. What can a viewer with only Can View reach?
cards.answer: Anything the page's datasets return when run with the publisher's data permissions, through tiles, filters, table views or exports.
cards.explanation: The catalog checks the publisher's grants, not the viewer's, so the page widens the publisher's access to every viewer. Publishing as a least-privilege service principal bounds that exposure to one table; publishing from a personal login with broad grants quietly shares them, and the grant leaves when the person does.

cards.prompt: Why is a refresh timestamp in the corner not enough to tell supervisors whether yesterday is in the numbers?
cards.answer: Because a refresh can run on time over old rows; readers need the period covered, the publish time and a not-updated wording.
cards.explanation: On a late morning the schedule still ran at 06:30 and its timestamp was true, yet it read Monday. A freshness line read from the publish-run table says which business day is shown and, when the job was late, says not updated in the same place, so the meeting decides knowingly.

cards.prompt: The nightly job finished at 08:20, but the page's schedule ran at 06:30 and posted a snapshot at 06:35. What did the channel receive?
cards.answer: The older day's rows, because the schedule read the table before the job published; only a freshness line inside the snapshot says so.
cards.explanation: A schedule re-runs the datasets over whatever the tables hold when it fires and knows nothing about the job; the supervisors' own queries at 07:45 also return Monday, because nothing newer has been published. Placing a dashboard task after the publishing task in the job, or a clock schedule with a reviewed buffer, fixes the order; the freshness line makes any remaining lateness visible.

cards.prompt: What does a metric view keep apart, and how does that stop the mean-of-rates error?
cards.answer: It keeps measure definitions apart from dimensions, so the ratio of sums is recomputed for whatever grouping the query asks for.
cards.explanation: Grouped by line, the measure returns 12 over 250 for line 3; with no grouping it returns 47 over 1,040 for the plant. Because the aggregation happens at query time from one governed definition, no dashboard author can average precomputed line rates by accident, and every SQL client reads the same formula.

cards.prompt: What does a supervisor need to read the morning page through Genie One, and what do they not need?
cards.answer: Consumer access, Can View on the published page and, because the page runs each viewer's own grants, SELECT on the accepted table.
cards.explanation: Genie One, previously Databricks One, is the business-user surface and consumer access is its least-privileged entitlement. The page itself is the same published object as in the workspace, so its permissions, its data-permission mode and its freshness line apply unchanged; only the surface differs.

cards.prompt: Which six fields does each storyboard frame carry, and how does a frame become an acceptance row?
cards.answer: Time, actor, surface, what is read, what is decided and where next; each frame's read value becomes an expected value to check.
cards.explanation: Frame 3 at 07:47 has supervisors comparing four tiles and choosing line 2 first; the acceptance script turns that into the four expected tile values. A storyboard that is only screenshots names no sentence and no decision, so it cannot expose a tile nobody reads or a not-updated morning nobody designed.

cards.prompt: Which properties of an AI/BI page do not travel to a Power BI or Tableau report built on the same table?
cards.answer: Its Can View list, its data-permission choice, its filters and defaults, its freshness line and its schedule.
cards.explanation: External tools connect to a SQL warehouse through a connector or an ODBC or JDBC driver and query tables and views under their own connection identity. Everything the page adds on top stays behind, so a Power BI report needs its own labels, sharing, refresh and acceptance rows, and an Import copy leaves the catalog's reach.

cards.prompt: Why must an acceptance script's expected values come from outside the page it checks?
cards.answer: Because values copied from the page always match it, so the script could never fail and would prove nothing.
cards.explanation: Cinderline's expected values come from the five-day reconciliation sheet: line 3 on day 4 is 4.8%, the plant with line 3 filtered stays 4.5%, and line 4 on day 5 reads no inspections. That independent source is how the run caught a 0.0% the contract forbids.
